utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone, including those in the field office. The -- may we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith again for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Appearing for Mr. Stanisic, Slobodan Cvijetic and Eugene O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Peric, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krgovic indicated he has about 20 minutes left, so I would invite him resume his cross-examination at this point. And, of course, I remind you you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Peric. Yesterday, if you remember, I showed you those criminal reports that were filed directly, as you explained, to the military prosecutor's office in Bijeljina concerning crimes committed in Teslic, and the criminal reports were filed by the police. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when you answered some questions by the Prosecutor and provided us with some mini-statistics about the reported persons from the area of Teslic, you did not include that number.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If we wanted to have a real picture of how many people were reported for what types of crimes, we would also need to have the log-book of this military court in Bijeljina, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the military court in Banja Luka, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Because criminal reports were filed to both criminal courts; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that there were criminal reports filed directly to them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Peric, I'd like to move to a different subject. In the former Yugoslavia, where you worked as a prosecutor, and in Republika Srpska, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, under Article 191, remand in custody could be ordered for a number of reasons. If you want to look at the Law on Criminal Procedure, it's P120 and your tab in the binder of Mr. Cvijetic is 23. Look at Article 191.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you found it, Your Honours? That's ERN 0025-2976.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It says remand in custody is always ordered against persons suspected of committing a crime for which the law prescribes a certain length sentence; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now turn the next page. And look at the other standards. In paragraph 2, item 1, if the person is hiding, or the identity cannot be determined, or, in the presence of other circumstances pointing to a risk of escape.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If there is a well-grounded suspicion that the person may destroy evidence or interfere with the investigation, intimidate witnesses, accomplices, or those hiding him.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Point 3: If particular circumstances indicate the person may continue the crime, complete the crime, or commit or execute a threat already issued.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If the crime committed is subject to a ten-year sentence of imprisonment, and the circumstances of the crime risk causing such a disturbance among the citizens, that may endanger the investigation and thus justifies remand in custody. Now, after a person is remanded in custody and then the investigating judge decides to terminate remand in custody within 30 days, that decision needs consent by the public prosecutor; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, in this specific case of the Mice Group, all the legal requirements for remand in custody were met for all those persons reported.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just help me from a technical point of view. Once remand in custody is ordered and investigation starts, this KI number is given to every decision made in the course of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every court decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In this specific case, the number under which procedure was taken against these persons for the crime in Teslic, the number is 35/92. Now look at P15312 [as interpreted] that's in the prosecutor's binder; tab 26.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Counsel, can you kindly repeat the number of that exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's P1312; tab 26 in the Prosecution binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Of which it has been removed, if I'm not wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] We removed it because I wasn't going to use it, but I think it's in Judge Peric's binder. And we can put it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And give the relevant numbers then, because it's not on the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's P1312.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, have you found it? Have you found this document? It's a decision to conduct investigation.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have another document here. But if I remember well, that's the right number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now let us go back to this Mice case you spoke about. The criminal report was filed against 16 persons, and the police arrested and brought before an investigating judge 16 persons; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The investigating judge, on the 16th of July, terminated remand in custody with your consent for three persons: Predrag Karagic, Mr. Tadic, and Mr. Subotic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw, I think, in the prison document that these persons were released on the basis of a certain court decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Look at tab 28 in the Prosecution's binder. It's P1314. That's a letter from the President of the high court. Look at the first sentence, where it says: "Under a subsequent decision from the investigating judge, release was ordered for Predrag Subotic, Zoran Tadic, and Predrag Karagic."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: There were no legal requirements for their release from custody.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If remand in custody was terminated, then the legal requirements existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were these persons members of the Mices Group?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the crime for which they were reported is certainly a serious crime, subject to a prison sentence of over ten years.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think they were permanent members of that group. I think they joined two or three days before the arrest and they had not been involved with all the other conduct with which the others were charged. You can check that in the decision to investigate. I know that Karagic was not based in Teslic. He was invited to come to Teslic. I think these three persons came just three days before the arrest. They're invited to join to work as a security detail or something. I think that was all considered and it was found there was no reason to keep them in custody.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think there is a small problem going on here. Nothing's on the screen at all. Oh, there we go. But what Mr. Krgovic read out, "under a subsequent decision from the investigating judge," I don't see those words anywhere. I see the words 16th July 1992, "An investigating judge ruled that detention be cancelled," but I don't see anything subsequent -- or anything as read out by Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it's not on the screen in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that -- were you reading that -- you were reading the second paragraph, were you? On the 16th -- which begins on 16th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. By a subsequent decision of the investigating judge, that's the beginning of the paragraph I read. Remand in custody was terminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We're talking here about a Mr. Karagic who is currently on trial before the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina for war crimes. I think he was convicted to 22 years.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was a trial, but I don't know if it was completed. I don't know whether he was charged with war crimes either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now please look at P1313. It's in the Prosecution binder, tab 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, the last name of this person is not "Karadzic"; it's Karagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please turn to page, in e-court, 30 and 30 in English. In your copy, the number in the right top corner is 04155935.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What number? What are the last four numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: 5935, in the right hand top corner.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Have you found it? Now turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Look at 151, 152, 153, 154, and 155, and 156. These are the Mices, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in the column on the right, on page 33, you will see, first, that they were transferred to the prison in Doboj on the 17th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it. Which column?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It's the first column; the date of placement in prison. The number on the page is 04155937. Just after the name.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Date of birth, place of birth, place of residence, date of imprisonment. Yes, can I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You see that they were remanded in custody by the lower court in Teslic, by decision KI 5/92.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they must have been remanded in custody earlier, because this is not a decision to remand them in custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now look at the next column. They were released on the 24th of July 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And they were released, all these persons mentioned on this page, based on -- or pursuant to the decision of the first instance court in Teslic, KI, as mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says. I suppose that there is a decision to release them from prison, but I have problems understanding the decision dated 11th of July, 1992, because that's not possible. They were arrested on the 1st, and they must have been placed in custody on the 3rd. Anyway, much earlier than this date, so I don't know what this is about. So if have you the decision we could take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have it on me at the moment. The problem is that earlier they were in police custody for three days?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that expired on 3rd of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And later on you will see from the criminal report the problem was the jurisdiction with regard to their arrest. So they were put up in the Kardijal, so they were not really in detention for a certain while.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, but it was detention, but only physically. They were not in prison. They were in Kardijal, but they could have -- could have been kept there only based on a relevant decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And Kardijal is a hotel at Vanja Vrucica [phoen], right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Teslic, that is correct. That's where they were kept for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So let us sum up Mr. Peric. All these persons I have mentioned, six persons on this page, were released based on a decision of the first instance court in Teslic, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that there is a decision on release from custody. This group of persons was not involved in most of the crimes committed by the group that belonged to the police, so that with regard to them, there were no more reasons to keep them in detention and that's why their custody was terminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, go back one page, please. That is page 0415935. And you will see these two person, Roboljub Sjilic [phoen], and Ranko Stjuka?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That's serial numbers 149 and 150. And these two were released pursuant to a decision of the first instance court in Teslic, file number KI 35/92.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. And probably they belonged to a military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have a reason to doubt the truthfulness of the information contained in this document, this log-book?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there is a decision on release of -- from detention of this group of military personnel, because they were not involved in most of the crimes committed by the members of this police formation. I believe that was the only reason, but we should check by looking at the decision and the reasons stated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: From this log-book it follows that the higher instance court in Doboj terminated detention for Pijunovic, Tekic, Culibrk, Djuric, and Spesevic [phoen]; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Pursuant to an appeal by defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In August 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Pursuant to an appeal by the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Talking about criminal reports against military personnel, isn't it true that this military wing of the Mice was reported for the execution of 40 Muslims at places outside Teslic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Some of them took part in the execution, but they admitted they did, which was established in the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, were there legal grounds for releasing this group of persons from detention with regard to the circumstances, because for murder the death penalty could be imposed and they -- it was required that they remain in detention.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that was a court decision. They were transferred to Doboj. Under the law, detention could be terminated after six months so that regardless of this legal requirement, with regard to the situation regarding their transfer to Doboj, detention would have been terminated anyway. They were transferred to Doboj to be released. This is obvious from the entire scenario of their transfer from Banja Luka. I even think that they were not really in prison, that they were only filed as being in prison, that they were on the list, but that they were actually at large.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: How did the release of the Mice affect the police and the persons who had arrested them? Namely, this group of hardboiled [as interpreted] criminals was at once at large again. How did that affect the work of the police? Very badly, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it affected the work of the police. In Doboj, this was hailed and celebrated in the streets. But to the people who had arrested them, probably were not delighted by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after that, there were threats to the people who had arrested them, specifically Mr. Radulovic and the others. You know about that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't. I suppose there may have been threats due to the circumstances of the arrest. You saw that there were injuries in the process, torture, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And such a court decision to release them and this attitude toward the arrest certainly discourages the police and undermines their work, because we saw that this case was perfectly processed and then the criminals were released.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is your conclusion. I need more context to comment. From this point of view, I cannot draw conclusions as to how this may have affected the police and the military psychologically or Teslic, Doboj, or Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You saw that brigade report that I showed which -- from which it follows that the soldiers from the brigade complain about the Mice re-appearing. It is a known fact that the Mice appeared again and started threatening the people who had arrested them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them came to Teslic and those were the reactions. But, at the time, I didn't even know that they were coming to Teslic again. But obviously they started reappearing in some situations. You must bear in mind that the relations between Teslic and Doboj throughout the war were very bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, let's me sum up and finish this topic. These people, even today -- or, rather, there are no proceedings against these people even today for the crimes they committed in Teslic; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is unfortunately true, with the exception of Karagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radulovic even today has problems because of this arrest and the investigation he conducted, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. Mr. Radulovic is an attorney nowadays, as far as I know, and I don't know of any problems, or his problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And these criminals who committed these offences are at large. And Mr. Radulovic is now an attorney, and Mr. Zupljanin, who ordered the arrest, is standing trial for the crimes of these Mice.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer. We didn't hear the answer to this last question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, apart from the fact that it's a comment and not a question. I don't know what the question was and I don't know what the answer was because we didn't get the translation. I didn't hear anything that Mr. Krgovic said at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about these facts about the result of all this, that the Mice are at large, Mr. Radulovic is no longer with the police, Mr. Zupljanin is standing trial -- Mr. Zupljanin who ordered the arrest of these Mice is standing trial for the crimes they committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, just a minute. That's not a question. It's a comment, and I object to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But is -- is what I said correct and true -- or, rather, do you know that? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's still a comment, and it's not a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naturally. Of course, I know. Today I'm certainly aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Peric. No more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic. Mr. Krgovic, please, could you assist me from where we have the evidence that Mr. Zupljanin ordered the arrests of the Mice Group?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Korner, please. Can I just reply to Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You can, but, Your Honour, it needs to be redacted; the whole speech by Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for this, I mentioned about the gentleman. Yes, I agree that this should be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, it should be redacted. My comment was just that I'm aware of the evidence that we had from previous witnesses. I just wanted to make sure that we have not received this evidence from this witness. That was my question. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honours, as a matter of interest, we haven't had that witness from any witness directly either. So it -- what Mr. Krgovic has said is not correct. Having said that, I anticipate that is the evidence that will be given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, the accused Zupljanin seems to be trying to get our attention. Perhaps his counsel. Is this -- Mr. Krgovic, is there --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't have further question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judge, first of all, I want to deal with the question of your resignation about which you were asked yesterday, and your interview was referred to by Mr. Cvijetic. I think we better just have that up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's page 4 of the second interview. Sorry. Oh, 65 ter 10359.02. And as it's -- the fourth, yes, the fourth page at the bottom. No, that's not it. Page 4, please. Yep.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page you were asked: What was the reason given why they wanted you removed? And you said: They gave several reasons. Amongst other things, they wrote that before the war I'd associated with a Muslim man who was a war criminal, and this was a young man I used to have a publishing house together with from Bosanski Brod. And I did associate with him before the war. He was a poet, he was a painter. And you go on to describe that. And then you said at the end of that paragraph: And this is the main reason they stated, for when they said that I wasn't a Serb, that I didn't support the state, and that I didn't support their politics or their policy. And could we go to the next page, please, the top of it. Then they said that I also wrote for Nin, and I remember them saying that I was the ideologist behind the creation of the socialist party in Teslic, that I was providing assistance to certain people within the socialist party, which is in fact true because there was a group of people within that party who were the opposition, the only opposition to the SDS and who had believed that the socialist party that Milosevic were against the SDS and they would have support from Belgrade. Was there any reason ever suggested ... you were not performing your duties properly as a public prosecutor? Not at all. There was not a single sentence in connection with work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Can we go back to the Judge. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judge Peric, you said that in interview in 2002. Was that your view at the time and is it your view today of why you were removed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is completely true. I saw that SDS document from Teslic. I wrote it in its entirety. It was brought to me by the chief prosecutor to show me who demands my removal and why. And that there had been several such letter and that he was saying to Karagic several times that I was a regular prosecutor and that there was no reason for him to remove him, and finally he was told, Either you remove Peric or I remove you, because I cannot cope with this Knezovic and the deputies from Teslic anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, that was reopened the question of your resignation by Mr. Cvijetic who showed you a document for which there was no translation available and read you a selected bit. And that's at page 10572 of the transcript. And the document, for which there is now a translation, is 1D277 -- sorry, it was at page -- I think it was at a later stage you were shown this document. Anyhow, can we have it up, please, 1D277. I don't think it was MFI'd at all. Was it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I thought it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what you said about it, Judge, when you were shown it, with the implication, I imagine, that you were corrupt, although it wasn't stated in those terms, because you were asked about the apartment that you got?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, it's page 10580 and 81 of the transcript yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you said Mr. Rade Pavlovic was a man who was not supporting the policies of the SDS. He openly fought against such policies. All the claims here about his criminal activities is untrue. The purpose of it was to discredit him and to dismiss him. He was a man with a reputation with authority who was protecting his employees of Bosniak and Croat nationality, and the SDS did not like this. I'm not interested in this, said Mr. Cvijetic, only the bit related to you. Well, now let's have a look at what is clear from the letter or the report I should say. Can we have it up on the screen, please. And go in it to the -- it will be the fourth page, please, in English. That's the bottom of page 3 of the English, I think. Sorry, can we go back one page in English, and I don't know where it is in B/C/S at all. Yes, that last paragraph, please. Page 4 of B/C/S. This is the report: After a litany of complaint about his alleged corrupt activities, in which you were dragged into it, his stance towards Muslims and Croats who are moving out voluntarily is rather unorthodox, especially in the current climate. He gives valuable gifts to more prominent Muslims and Croats who are leaving as a sign of gratitude, in inverted commas, for everything they have given to Teslic. In these circumstances, he never fails to apologise to the Muslims and Croats for having to leave their hearths, adding that there are many Serbs who regret their leaving. Because of such actions on his part Radio Tesanj has -- Could we go to the next page. -- has been of late referring to Pavlovic as the most humane Serb and in other laudatory terms. Is that, Judge Peric, what you were referring to when you give that answer to Mr. Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Pavlovic was really an honourable man who want to help people, and I also wanted to help Pavlovic for that apartment to be preserved for the people who had renovated it and lived in it. That was a complete lie. If that was an official police report, you can see what the police were dealing with. Pavlovic was never accused or suspected. They tried to remove him after the war. They circled his company and there was a clash between the workers and the police, and he was -- he was a nuisance to many people, but such reports were a complete fabrication.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: On page 16, line 13, of the current transcript the first word should be "read," "I read it in its entirety."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know whether Your Honours want this to be exhibited. Your Honours, I do say that it would have been proper for Mr. Cvijetic, knowing there was no translation and having heard the answer the Judge, to have referred him there and then or at least us to that paragraph. Now, can I -- as I say, I don't know whether Your Honours think this is something that you want to have exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Inasmuch as it was -- one of the lines of the cross-examination was to attack the credibility and honesty of this witness, and this was a document relied on, in order to give a context to that bit of evidence I should it should be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then, Your Honours now that we've got the translation, Your Honours have seen exactly what this is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the -- as I said, my recollection is that it was marked for identification so -- yes, so it would -- that -- that would now be lifted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I move then, Judge Peric, to another matter that you were asked about Mr. Cvijetic, and this is at page 10560 of the transcript. You were being taken through the Criminal Code and the duties of a prosecutor. And --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I just want to make sure I've got the... yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it was put to you that citizens -- you were asked question at the top of page: Were you ever in a situation as a public prosecutor that a citizen comes to you and verbally tells that you a crime was committed and that he or she wants the proceeding to be launched against the perpetrator? No. I've been a prosecutor for three years and I was a prosecutor for three years, I've never been in such a situation. Citizens normally report crimes to the police and never has any citizen come to me to report a crime. Now, first, leaving that aside for a moment, supposing a citizen had filed a criminal report with you, what would you have to do with that criminal report? Who would be -- would have to investigate whether there was substance to this report?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police, of course. What I would do with the report is write a letter to the police and ask police inspectors to collect information related to that report, to question certain persons, et cetera. Simply collect evidence. I, as a prosecutor, could not do that. I could possibly invite some persons to talk to them, but this was mostly done through the police. And this procedure applies to date. Even the minister would ask the police and other agencies to provide logistical support in collecting evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You say you never ever had a citizen reporting a crime to you in the whole of your three years as a prosecutor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It's simply part of our legal culture. It is the police to which crimes are reported and it is the police that enforces security, protects public order and morale.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next, can I move to another matter that you were asked about. And that was the processing, if you like, of an investigation. It was put to you: Mr. Peric, let me summarise the position of the Defence in relation to the implementation of the provisions you were looking at. The prosecution of the perpetrators and their processing before the judicial organs at the time was exclusively part of the authorities of the public prosecutor, and then further processing would be under the authority of the relevant court. And your reply was: Prosecution, yes, but preparation and collection of evidence was something that had -- was to be done by the police. One must make a distinction here. So effectively, who conducted the first investigation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Preliminary investigation in the pre-indictment stage was always handled by the police. Always. And the results of these pre-indictment steps were submitted to the prosecutor, either in the form of a criminal report or by briefing the prosecutor about the steps that had been taken, especially if they found there were no elements of crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police had a service, the Criminal Investigation Service, which had its chief, and this service dealt exclusively with the discovery of crime and collection of evidence. That was a special service within the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, once an investigative judge had become involved, who would he have to rely on, for example, to arrest the perpetrators of the alleged crimes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the police, of course, and only the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who would be responsible for locating the witnesses to the crimes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police, of course. They would have to find out his or her address, bring him or her in, or even deliver a subpoena regarding persons who did not want to appear in court. They had to rely solely on the police. Otherwise, they would be unable to do their job.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was that the same in respect of the conduct of searches and the seizure of evidence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. All the searches, all crime scene investigations. Everything was done with the help of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a moment of your time. Perhaps it would be fair to ask the witness on whose orders and under whose supervision the police did that work when a case was in the stage of investigation and who led all these procedures.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The prosecutor gives authority to the police, unless he leads a particular investigating step. He could, for instance, take charge of a crime scene investigation, but he could also assign his authority to the police and did not normally take part in those investigative steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Korner asked you who orders these steps to be taken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The investigating judge does not --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I truly object to this. I'm in the middle of re-examination and suddenly Mr. Cvijetic gets up again to continue his cross-examination. I mean -- this is outrageous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I agree, Ms. Korner. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but Your Honours I -- I'm sorry, would Your Honour like to point out to Mr. Cvijetic it's utterly improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I must explain with all due respect that the witness has to be asked a fair question. The witness was led to give a wrong answer. Well, only now did he give an answer that is in conformity with the law. If we go on with questioning of this kind, we will not get to the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do apologise. I just have an intervention to the transcript. It's page 21, line 18, beginning with the word "They had to rely," actually witness said, "the prosecution had to rely solely on police." That was his word. Maybe my learned friend, Ms. Korner, can clarify that with the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that right, Judge Peric? Did you say the prosecution had to rely. I understood you to say -- I was asking you -- can I make this absolutely clear, the questions I asking related to once the investigating judge was in charge of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So I was not misleading the witness, and I take strong objection to Mr. Cvijetic's intervention at any stage in the middle of re-examination. Now, I was asking specific questions about the time at which the investigative judge became involved. On whom the investigative judge had to rely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Judge Peric, I'm sorry for this somewhat unseemly interruption but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's wait for the witness to answer to be clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just about to go back to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologies. Judge answered on your question, it was line 5: "Is that right, Judge Peric? Did you say the prosecution had to rely ..." and then he said, "yes," but it was not in the transcript so maybe you can ask him again in relation to my objection to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judge Peric, when you were answering my questions - and I will go back to the actual question and answer - I've forgotten what line you said it was, now. 21, line 19. Right. And I'll go back and read the whole series to you. My question was: "Now once an investigative judge has become involved, who would he have to rely on, for example, to arrest the perpetrators of the alleged crimes?" And your answer was: "On the police, of course, and only the police." "Q. Who would be responsible for locating the witnesses to the crimes?" "A. The police, of course. They would have to find out his or her address, bring him or her in, or even deliver a subpoena regarding the person who is did not want to appear in court. They had to rely solely on the police." Now did you say then instead of "they," "the prosecution"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can clarify. Everyone relies on the police. The prosecutor, the investigating judge, and even the court, during trial, if it is necessary to ensure the presence of a witness. At all stages, only the police for the prosecutor and for the court and for the judge, the police is the supporting body, the force that supports their work at all stages.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. And one final question on this topic before I move to the next. Is -- at what stage does an investigation become a prosecution?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the request to conduct an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At that stage it's a prosecution as opposed to an investigation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That's correct. Those are criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honours. And I've lost track of when -- is that about the time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No, we have a ways to go yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Yes, I'm sorry. I've slightly lost track this morning. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I then next move to the question, you were asked by, I believe, Mr. Krgovic, this was, about the attacks on Stenjak and Rankovici, of the operations which is 10957. Page 10957 in the transcript. I apologies, 10597, yes. Yes, yes. You were asked about by Mr. Krgovic about the military operations in Stenjak and Rankovici. And it was put to you that you don't know anything about the reasons for the operation or the causes of the operation; 10598. And you said: Yes, that's correct, I don't know anything about the details. Now, I think we better clarify that because you were asked about this in your interview, second interview at page 71. You were asked, first of all, about Stenjak, and you described the attack -- perhaps we better have the page up. Page 71 of this interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The investigator said he was going to ask you about the military operations in Stenjak and Rankovici. And you explained that it was a large village, inhabited exclusively by Muslims, and you were asked: Did you actually see the tank firing on Stenjak, and you said that you heard it because it was about 2 to 3 [sic] metres away from the Court. And then it was one tank or is that other fire coming from places. And you said, I think there was another one firing from the direction of what is called the cattle market? Was there any response, you were asked, any firing from the village. I couldn't see that nor do I know that. I am not aware of any resistance being put up. I never heard anything about it, but I remember hearing that people said many people had left the village before the attack. And, next page, please. You were asked, at the top of the page, next page. So why do you think there was a military -- military operation carried out there then. Your answer was intimidation, to set an example for other villages. Then you were asked about the shells. And you said you didn't see that anything was destroyed. Did the infantry enter Stenjak, you were asked. And you said, yes, I think it was the military and police groups that entered, and I think that several people were killed. I was -- I was told by -- about this by the people who actually buried those people who got killed, and I think they couldn't even establish the identity of two or three people who were killed. And then you were asked if you knew had killed them, and you said no. And then you were asked about Rankovici. Now, first of all, dealing alone with Stenjak, that evidence that you gave then or -- sorry, that information you gave then, was that your recollection and understanding at the time that you gave this interview?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it. But I meant direct knowledge before that action. That it would happen. Later, I heard about several dead who could be identified. I heard the fire, because it was very close. I saw the tank and the fire from the tank -- I heard the fire from the tank.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The dead who could not be identified.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So when you were answering Mr. Krgovic's questions, you were dealing with the direct -- whether you had direct information?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you, yourself, heard the tank firing at the time of the -- the -- the attack on the village?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard of the tank. I perhaps even saw it because it was 200 metres away from the court-house by the road to Doboj. Stenjak is a town neighbourhood. It's very central.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then you moved on -- you were then asked about Rankovici. If we just go back to the interview for a moment, the same page. You then -- you thought it was on the 8th or 12th of May, and then you corrected that to say it was June, later on. And then at the bottom of the page you were asked, before we cover Rankovici, do you think there's any relationship between the arrival of the Mices and the attack on Stenjak. And you -- it said, yes [sic], of course, it was their action, operation. And then over the next page. How [sic] do you mean it was their operation. They participated in the same [sic] thing -- sorry, the whole thing. It was part of their strategy of installing order. You were asked how did they participate. I don't know. And then the tanks, they didn't arrive with tanks, they were regular army tanks. No, they came to the brigade, to Bilanovic and Petricevic - I'm sorry, that one I have a real difficulty with - was his duty, and it was all co-ordinated with the Crisis Staff. They brought them in and arranged for everything. They were just a tool in the strategy of the Crisis Staff. Let's talk about the attack on Rankovici. It was after the attack of Stenjak; correct. Yes. Can you describe the military operation that had happened in that village. I can. Whatever I can tell you comes from the investigation we conducted. Apparently, somebody from that village shot -- fired shots at police or a military patrol. I don't know whether that's true or not. Maybe this was just a way for them to justify their operation, but they put that down as the reason for the operation. And then the police and the army went there. It was the same as in Stenjak. It was a co-ordinated action. Just in case the police, both the police and army. And in this operation on Rankovici, one of the Mice was wounded and one policeman or one man was killed. And then you describe what happened afterwards. So was this your conclusion, having investigated this matter as to how this attack came about?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All that I said was based on what I heard during the investigations we conducted at the court. I did not see anything with my own eyes, and I did not participate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when you talk about the -- a joint operation between the military and the police, are you just talking about the Mices or other members outside the Mices, or both the military and the police?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The local police was involved, the Mices, and the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then you were asked, over the page, just very briefly -- sorry, can we go back to ... Yep. And then you talked about the interrogations you carried out. You talked about what happened to the village -- the people who had been in the village. You said Rankovici was a village exclusively inhabited by Muslims. And you were asked then, were the Croats -- where were the Croats based largely. And you said, after this operation on Rankovici there was a similar operation done on the village of Komusina where the Catholic church is and the holy edifice as well. The Croatian villages gravitated toward the Zenica municipal boundaries. So their town was towards the end when the inside operations were finished. And was that again something you discovered as a result of your investigations into the Mice?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened later. And that's also indirect knowledge on my part, regarding actions or people who participated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember this arises from my cross-examination. I don't remember mentioning Komusina and this operation. We talked about two operations, Rankovici and Stenjak.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I understand it, the suggest -- I know those are the only two villages mentioned, but the suggestion was that in each case the judge was unaware of the actual nature of these operations with which, on the face of it, the judge agreed, which is why I was dealing with all of them, and the three operations run as one, even though specifically Komusina wasn't mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Perhaps you should confine yourself to the [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I dealt with the topic in any event.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I move, please, to the next matter that was put to you, namely, that after the Mice were arrested in July, and this is at page 10599, you said, in the period when the people from Banja Luka were there, all Muslims and Croats that were in detention at different locations were released with the exception of several against whom indicts were issued and they were still being prosecuted. Now from whom did you get the information that all of these people who had been arrested by the Mice and were being held in various detention places were released?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Got it from Radulovic Predrag. Together with him, I went to the prison of the Territorial Defence because he invited me to be present at the disbanding of that prison. So I came together with him to that prison and was present when the detainees were released and regarding other prison, I heard from him they were disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So the only one that you're aware of where you actually saw people -- or you were present when people were released was the one in the Territorial Defence building. And for the rest, you're relying on information that Mr. Radulovic gave you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, Your Honours, I think that is now time for the break because I'm moving to a marginally different topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It will take me more than five minutes. But, Your Honours, as I say, I completely lost track of when we're having breaks at moment, but I'm perfectly happy to go on for another five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If it will take you more than five minutes, we can conveniently take the break at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As a matter of interest, Ms. Korner, how much longer do you think you would be in total in your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No more than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judge, just a couple more questions about the -- these detention places. Were you aware that -- that there was a -- a detention facility at Pribinic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. There was even before the arrival of the Mice and I believe that it was closed down, but it was re-opened when the Mice came, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Were you aware that people were actually kept there until the 5th -- at least the 5th of October?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot assert that with certainty. It's a -- it's possible, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And were you aware of another detention facility at the partisan handball place?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a sort of open-air collection centre. It was not a usual prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I absolutely agree with you. But were you aware, again, that apparently people were detained there, non-Serbs, until at least the 20th of October?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment this time reference, but I know that it existed, and I saw people there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, as I said, I wanted to move to another topic that you were asked about. It was put to you effectively that when you were looking -- when you were asked to look again at your report for September - perhaps you'd better have that. It's in tab 84 for you, Judge, and the number is P1353.15. And effectively you were asked about the section which is on -- just a moment ... find it myself. I think it's page 1, and you were asked about the relationship between -- yes. It's the last paragraph of -- paragraph 1, the introduction. Relations between the public prosecutor's office and the public security station were within the limits of correctness and professionalism, although they were marked by subjective organisational weaknesses in one period. And at page 10604, you were asked by Mr. Krgovic: Were you referring to the time when the Mices were in Teslic. And you said: Yes, that's the period I had in mind. And then in the period after that, covered by your report, your relations were good. Yes, concerning the criminal reports that arrived, the co-operation with regard to them was good. Now, you told us yesterday -- when I was asking you questions in-chief, that the police were not, in fact, reporting crimes to you. I think I better find my actual question. I think you said it in your interview as well. When you talked about relations being bad during the period of the Mice, were you referring to reports of crimes being not given to you at all, obviously; or were you referring to something else? What did you mean by "relations were good"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This statement of mine refers to those cases that were processed and good cooperation with regard to the cases or files that were forwarded to the prosecutor's office. With regard to that, the relations were good. All the reports were professional, contained enough evidence, and professionally done. That's what I meant. Everything in connection with those reports was all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see. Right. That's -- so it's in the reports that you actually submitted. All right. Thank you. That's clarified that. Thank you very much. You were then -- it was put to you, and you agreed with it, and this is on page 10603 of the transcript, that the main complaint about crimes committed pertains to the army. And you said: Yes, that was the greatest problem. The army did not have a -- doesn't quite make sense in the transcript, but did not organise, I think it should be "organised" the military police and did nothing to exert control over the armed persons while those people were not at the front line. You told the Court when I was asking you question about the type of people that were being prosecuted, that I think that the people processed were criminals of classical type so to speak, this is page 10537 of the transcript, and in the case where the people weren't prosecuted, these were people either that were under the control of the police, or the case was that maybe the police didn't want them to be prosecuted. That's the only conclusion I can reach. Now, were the -- the crimes only committed by those who were in the military; or were there also those not in the military committing crimes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my conclusion also. Whatever was not reported and investigated, I suppose that was, in a way, under the control of either the police or the military, or both. I cannot strictly distinguish between the military and the police. I believe that there was some sort of joint action. After all, both the commander and the chief of police were members of the Crisis Staff, so they had to know about all these events. I concluded from all that that cases of common crime were being investigated, whereas other crimes were under some sort of control of either the police or the military, or they were tolerated from a political level. These -- these were my conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then, really, finally, you were asked a number of questions in relation to the entries in your register which show the arrest of Serbs for crimes committed against non-Serbs. And you were also -- it was effectively put to you that the arrests of Croats and Muslims stopped once the Mice were out. Now, in relation to the second aspect - that is, the arrest of Croats and Muslims stopped once the Mice were removed - is that actually right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, but only applies to the period where -- while the police from Banja Luka was there and carried out policing in Teslic. After that, things went bad again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And as -- it's right, I think, we can see from the KT log-book, in fact, that there were further prosecutions of Muslims and Croats for such things as armed rebellion and illegal possession of weapons. Yes. Thank you very much, indeed, Judge Peric, for coming. That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Judge Peric, when you are to deal with a group of criminals and when proceedings are started against them, you normally proceed against every member of the group, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Was there any decision ordering the arrest of Mr. Savic, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no such decision. We never received one from the police. I don't know what exactly the explanation was. Mr. Radulovic could say more about that. I don't know why he was not included in the criminal report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The fact that he was not in Teslic, that he couldn't be found in Teslic, has nothing to do with the question whether there are investigations, whether there are proceedings against him or not. The fact that he is not there, not in Teslic, or cannot be found, does not prevent investigations to be started against someone, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But I believe that, at that moment, it wouldn't have been possible to arrest him because he was in Doboj under the control of the people who had sent him to Teslic. So for those reasons at that moment we didn't carry out investigative measures with regard to him. Instead, we waited for a more convenient moment. That's the only reason I can mention. I don't know why he was left out. It -- it was Predrag Radulovic and the police who didn't include him in the criminal report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And if I'm not wrong, the same goes for, I don't recall his name, but head of the military part of the group; is that right? What was his name Petricevic or something like that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Ljubisa Petricevic. The explanation for him that we received -- got for him was that he was taken to detention to Banja Luka by the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. I also have just one small question for you. And my question relates to your testimony -- or not your testimony, sorry, your interview with the Prosecution on the 10th of January, 2002. And I don't know whether it's possible to bring up these statements on the screen. I would like you to see what, in the English version, is page 7 of your statements to the Prosecution of 10th January, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is possible to bring it up. It's 10359.02. Tab 76 for the Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Are you there, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. He doesn't have it because it wasn't in B/C/S. He listened to the tapes. It.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But it is up on the screen, and if Your Honour reads it out in English, it will be translated to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Judge, what I wanted to raise with you was the issue of political pressure that was put on your office. And speak about this at several places in your statement, and one of these places is on page 7, and I will read out slowly to you what you said. It was Ms. Korner who asked you whether what you told at the first interview was right; namely - and this is a quotation of what you said: "Most important was the pressure exerted on the police in criminal, in that role, in criminal proceedings. Control exerted by the political parties, in this case, the SDS. What were" - and this is Ms. Korner's question to you - "what were, in your experience, happening between May 1992 and roughly September or October 1992, what sort of control was being brought on the police." And your answer was: "The chief of police was member of the Crisis Staff, and they had meetings every morning. And they controlled the entire situation on the territory of the municipalities. So, all the members of the Crisis Staff knew what happened. And all the members of the Crisis Staff could influence the chief of police as to what he would do. I even think they asked the police to perform certain duties which did not fall into the police duties and, on the other hand, do not imply what the police should have done." Judge, this was your response to Ms. Korner's questions at the time, and I would like to follow up on your answer. Could you tell us a bit about the political pressure that was being put on the police. And my question would be: Was your office also under some sort of pressure from the political level?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. What you read is my statement and I still think today that influence was exerted on the police and that the police was under political pressure. The chief of police was, I believe, at the same time, the president of the SDS of Teslic, and he was a member of the Crisis Staff. He knew -- he had access to information and could exert influence on the police. When I said at the first meeting of -- that we didn't want to take part in the work of the Crisis Staff and that we didn't want to be involved in politics in any way, they left us in peace. They left us alone. Only once was I called up to bring some file to the municipality, and I answered that, And this is the last time you're asking something like that from me. But taking into consideration the huge number of unprocessed cases, I believe that it was the position of the Crisis Staff that some cases should not be investigated and, what's more, that some things should be done in contravention of the law. But these are my conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks. But, Judge, when you say that political pressure was also put on the prosecutor's office, could you tell us a little more about just how that pressure was exerted? You -- you seemed to have indicated just now that you were left alone, and yet, in your previous answer, you seem to imply that political pressure was, indeed, put on you. So how was this political pressure applied?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained those were attempts of political influence and pressure. I mentioned the case when we were invited to a meeting of the Crisis Staff; and the second time I was asked to bring a file to the president of the municipality; and the third indirect sort of pressure was they wanted to remove me. But there was no other political pressure on the public prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So your testimony today is that the political pressure that was exerted was mainly on the police and not directly on the prosecutor's office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well then. So your assertion that the police was under pressure, under political pressure, is based on your observation that the chief of police was member of the Crisis Staff. Is that the way we should understand it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A member of the Crisis Staff and the President of the political party that had absolute power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right so this leads to the next question. Who was formulating the political pressure? Was that the political party that you have just spoken of, the SDS; or was it in a wider sense, the Crisis Staff? Are you able to make that distinction, if such a distinction exists?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was the political party, the SDS who had the dominant influences and the deputies who were members of that party. If we want to establish a hierarchical connection, then it's the SDS, the political party that was the ruling party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So I understand that the SDS was controlling the political priorities of the Crisis Staff in Teslic. Is that -- that the way we should take this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the political priorities of the highest government level and the local level. They were -- they belonged to the same political party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What do you know exactly of this policy of the SDS at the time? Do you -- are you able to form an opinion about whether it was a distinct and clear policy of the SDS to remove non-Serbs from Teslic and its nearby villages?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never been able to make a conclusion as to the official policy of the SDS. It was never published anywhere. You could only draw conclusions from what you observed or from what was happening in reality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And so your conclusion then is, that, based on the events as they happened on the ground, you infer that it must have been the policy of the SDS to have non-Serbs removed from the area. Is that a correct reflection of your opinion?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Now, this policy that was then, in your view, applied by the SDS in -- in Teslic, do you know if this was a policy that also applied in -- in Doboj and Banja Luka and other municipalities? Or maybe throughout the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be certain. I believe that there were differences between municipalities. There were some municipalities that were considered extreme, that -- where was extreme nationalism and in others there were no extreme occurrences so that the situation was rather varied. Doboj was considered one of the extreme municipalities, and it's still considered one, in which the SDS has strong influence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's get back to Teslic. Do you know if any objections to the policy was ever raised in the Crisis Staff in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only objections were outside the institutions, non-institutional, because there was no political opposition. Only people such as Rade Pavlovic and others who fought their own private war against these structures and were rather successful in opposing them but it wasn't very significant. But I haven't heard of any public or institutionalised resistance or reactions or opposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, suppose someone from the police, or the army, didn't want to go along with the priorities handed down by the Crisis Staff, then what would happen? I mean, were you ever aware of any such differences in opinion?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that person would certainly be removed from their position. I believe there were cases like that, although I can't remember any particular ones now. There were many dismissals, removal, replacements, brigade commanders were removed. New ones were brought in. The situation was pretty chaotic. I don't know any details, but I suppose anyone who didn't think the same had to tow the line or they would be removed, or called up to the army, like I was, after my dismissal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Now, finally, I would be grateful if you could explain to us - if you know - a bit about the relations between the Crisis Staff and -- and the army. And the reason I'm putting this question is that, ordinarily, after the declaration of an imminent threat of war, one would assume that the -- that the army was in control of all activities in the area, yet you seem to suggest that it was really the Crisis Staff that was controlling events in the areas. So, you know, it couldn't be both ways. Either it was the army who decided and the army would then have taken control over -- and authority over the police, or it was the Crisis Staff. How was this dual authority exercised in -- in real terms; do you know?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'll try. I think Teslic was a rather peculiar case in that sense. The army did not have control over the Crisis Staff. On the other hand, the Crisis Staff -- sorry, the SDS tried to control the army through the Crisis Staff and officers inclined towards the SDS were made brigade commanders, and there was constantly talk that Teslic needs commanders who were natives of Teslic rather than commanders from outside. I know that former JNA officers were not popular because they were thought to be closer to the socialist party and that they were not patriotic enough. I think the Crisis Staff had the key role rather than brigade commanders in the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. That's all I have to ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I have leave to ask a few questions after the Judges' questions, questions put by Judge Harhoff specifically, a few clarifications to be precise. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Krgovic:

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Peric when you are answering questions put by honourable Judge Harhoff you were talking about the work of the Crisis Staff and its composition. Isn't it true that in July, or starting with July the Crisis Staff no longer existed and the Assembly of the municipality of Teslic operated regularly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the Crisis Staff existed throughout the war. It was called the Crisis Staff and then the War Staff and it existed in parallel with the Assembly. The Assembly was like a democratic embassy of sorts. It didn't decide on anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you haven't seen a single decision of the Crisis Staff in Teslic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure such decisions existed and these people sat every day, and they made decisions rather than the parliament. The parliament, when it made decisions, made decisions that they had formulated previously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you look at 65 ter 866. It's in my binder --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Krgovic. The transcript -- you have to keep an eye on the screen. The translation was still continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the Zupljanin Defence binder, tab 4. This is, Mr. Peric, an excerpt from the minutes of the Assembly session held on 20th August.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You can see what the discussion was about, you can see who participated, and you can see there is reference to the same thing you mentioned on page 1, where they endorse the agenda -- sorry, the minutes of the previous Assembly session, and the conclusion of the Assembly that the military police at battalion level was not doing its job. That's on page 1. And after that, please look at page 6 where Mr. Perisic, in his contribution, says that the issue of paramilitary units has to be dealt with, and he proposes to the military command to arrest and started proceedings against any brigade members involved in illegal activities, and you can see the other persons who respond, the previous chief of police, Kuzmanovic, and Djordjevic, and all these differences of opinion at the Assembly session. Isn't it the case that from the month of July the Assembly met regularly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It held sessions but in parallel with the Crisis Staff. And I believe the Assembly was used exclusively for mutual settlements of accounts between the chief of the Crisis Staff, the brigade commander, Perisic, the Assembly was supposed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sorry, Judge Peric, I just want to intervene with counsel. You do appreciate that the document we now have on the screen is under seal, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Probably Your Honour, I didn't -- I really -- I didn't notice that. What's the position of Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- I have to confess I had forgotten that as well. But it needs to come off the screen, and that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Necessary instructions have been conveyed to the AV unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I really didn't mean to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, broadly speaking, can you tell us if you have ever seen after July, and you brought some documents to the Prosecution during your interview, documents you had in your possession. But after the month of July 1992, did you ever see a decision of the Crisis Staff published or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were such decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure, but I think there were such decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What content? What did they relate to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely these issues that were first discussed at the Crisis Staff and then they passed through the Assembly. And you can see in these minutes all the people from the Crisis Staff sitting at the Assembly session. Jokic, Markovic, Kuzmanovic, and others, they're all sitting in the Assembly, and they are the same people who made decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Markovic at the time was not on the police force. He was not police commander. Kuzmanovic either.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the minutes that you referred me to, in paragraph 3, look at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, haven't you made your point within the context of the -- what arose directly out of the questions of Judge Harhoff? Aren't you wondering ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I have only one question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just answer with a yes or no. Have you ever seen or known about a decision signed Crisis Staff, after, after the month of July 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure, I believe it was even the War Staff and the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Peric. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't suppose the Prosecution have anything arising out the Judge Harhoff's questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Judge Peric, we thank you for your attendance before the Tribunal and assisting us with respect to your testimony. You are now released as a witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I assume that there is nothing that need engage our attention before I take the adjournment for the weekend?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is.
