If you recall, I said I would like to ask Your Honours to reconsider Your Honours' ruling in respect of the articles, and I would like to take the opportunity, really, to deal with the whole question of hearsay, because as Your Honours know, we were taken by surprise, first of all, by Mr. O'Sullivan's general submission and secondly by Your Honours ruling. And so, I'm sorry, I know it's Friday, but I would like to take a little time, because we've got a bit of time which we won't have next week. If I could, I would be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Are you ready to begin?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am, yes. Your Honours, it seems to me that effectively because this is an ongoing saga, I ought to deal with Mr. O'Sullivan's really general submission although he has related it specifically to the documents produced by Mr. Traynor about this question of the admission into evidence of newspaper articles. As Your Honour says, you have in some cases admitted them and in others not, but the general principle, as Your Honours are perfectly well aware, is set out under Rule 89 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and which has been interpreted on a number of occasions, that, under Rule 89(A), a Chamber shall apply the rules of evidence set forth in the section and not bound by national rules; and (C) ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, before you expand on that, our ruling was -- was not -- was in no way upon Mr. O'Sullivan's objection. The reasons why we ruled as we did had nothing to do with Mr. O'Sullivan's objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I perfectly understand that Your Honours, I do. I'm simply, as it were, using the opportunity just to deal with the general principle because it's our submission that it wasn't perhaps altogether properly enunciated by Mr. O'Sullivan, as I say. And I will come on to the reasons Your Honours' ruling why we're asking for reconsideration. Your Honours, in (C): "A Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value." I know I'm repeating the obvious. Your Honour, that includes hearsay. But the various cases on hearsay do not distinguish between, as Mr. O'Sullivan put it, admissible hearsay and inadmissible hearsay. There is no such distinction in the authorities on the matter. The key factor for the admission of hearsay evidence is that of reliability. Your Honours, there have been three appeals decisions, decision on this matter, none of them -- and Your Honour, may I say straight away to Ms. Frew, who did the research for me while I was slightly otherwise occupied. There is no specific case which has dealt with newspaper articles as such. The hearsay cases are all on slightly different aspects. But Aleksovski was the first in 1999, Kordic, which was not referred to by Mr. O'Sullivan, was the second in 2000, and Milosevic was the third of the three cases, all decided before Milutinovic in which Mr. O'Sullivan was counsel. The Milosevic decision is the 30th of September, 2002. And, in effect -- Your Honour, the situation there, just to set that out, related to a statement which had been taken from a dead -- sorry, a dead witness. Not taken from -- the witness from whom the witness had been taken from had died before the trial. And the question was whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't believe that's Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's Kordic. You`re quite right. Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. I'm muddling up with Kordic. The Milosevic case was the -- sorry, Your Honours, just let me ... Yes, the application was in relation to -- I'm so sorry. It was an investigator giving evidence which was a summary of a large number of witness statements. The Kordic one was the dead witness. In any event, the trial -- the Appeals Chamber went through the previous authorities including those of Aleksovski and quoted Aleksovski at page 6 of the Judgement and said that hearsay evidence -- the Chamber is given a broad discretion to admit relevant hearsay evidence, that it's admitted to prove the truth of its contents. Like me, Ms. Pidwell, had not had a chance to research the authorities before she stated that it was not being put forward for the truth of the contents. That it should be admitted. It's been shown to be reliable. And it's for this purpose the Chamber may consider both the content of the hearsay statement and the circumstances under which the evidence arose, (E) of the probative value of a hearsay statement will depend upon the context and character of the evidence in question. The Appeals Chamber also stated that the absence of opportunity to cross-examine the person who made the statements and whether the hearsay is first-hand or more removed are relevant to the probative value. And I emphasise that. It's also acknowledged that though it depends on infinitely variable circumstances of the particular case, the weight or probative value to be afforded to hearsay evidence will usually be less than that given to a testimony of a witness who has given it under a form of oath and has been cross-examined. And that goes without saying. But that doesn't prevent it in any way from being admissible. The court went on, the Appeals Chamber, went on to say that the reliability and this is at top of page 7 of the hearsay statement is relevant to its admissibility and not just to its weight. And then at -- it dealt with statements for the purpose of legal proceedings, which is not something that's relevant to this particular issue. And then at paragraph 22 it approved -- it proved the following: "As stated in the Aleksovski decision, the passage on which the Prosecution did not rely, the Chamber must first consider whether the summary is first-hand hearsay; that is, whether the persons who made the statement summarised personally saw or heard the events recorded in their statements, and whether the absence of the opportunity to cross-examine those persons affects the reliability. "According to the submission of the Prosecution, the opportunity to cross-examine the person who summarised those statements does not overcome the absence of opportunity to cross-examine the persons who made them. In different cases, of course, the statements may contain their own indicia of reliability which does overcome the absence of that opportunity." Now, Your Honours, the -- Mr. O'Sullivan relied very heavily on the decisions in Milutinovic. There were in fact a total of three of them. The first on the 1st of September, 2006; on the 8th of September, 2006; and then on the 29th of November, 2007, although the last was in relation to newspaper articles. I'll come back to that. And the first two were in relation to the witnesses who had prepared a report one was called Mitchell and Abrahams -- or two were called Mitchell and Abrahams, and somebody was called Hax -- a completely unpronounceable name, Haxhibeqiri, H-a-x-h-i-b-e-q-i-r-i.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That would be Haxhibeqiri.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, of course, you'd be there so you'd know how to pronounce it. I'm not even going to attempt to pronounce that one. Your Honour, they were all people who were called to talk about publicly a report, Mitchell and Abrahams, that had been done by OSCE on Kosovo. It was called "Kosovo as Seen as Told." And the report contained extracts from a number of people who had been interviewed but who had not been interviewed by these two witnesses personally. And that was the distinction, the very great distinction which Mr. O'Sullivan didn't refer to between that and where you're interviewing the people who'd give you the information. They were unable to say who had actually interviewed them because it was just a report and had not themselves spoken to the witnesses. Your Honour, so there is the, we submit, the great distinction between that case and the ones -- the one that Your Honour was dealing with. In the third judgement, which was an admission of documents from the bar table, this was an article from the "Politika" newspaper, and this was the Chamber's decision. All of these, of course, are discretionary decisions, and not in the way that an Appeals Chamber decision is a binding. "The Chamber has previously indicated it will not generally consider newspaper articles admissible solely to prove the truth of their contents." And they went on to deal with that. Now, Your Honours those are the authorities and that's the background to this, and we say that the test is, as the Appeals Chamber enunciated, looking at the surrounding circumstances, is the information -- is it reliable information which we can admit. And it doesn't matter whether it's first-hand or second-hand hearsay. Now, Your Honours, that's the background to this case or to -- to -- to Mr. Traynor. And can I just add one further thing on this, because I raised this because Mr. Pantelic, in his eloquent address at the end of the day, nothing to do with adjudicated facts and what Your Honours should do about that, which was a totally different subject to that under discussion, said that, in -- in discussing JCE he said that -- this is page 10469 of the transcript, that the honourable Judge Agius who was quite, I would say, he was an excellent judge, found Brdjanin discussing the issue of JCE. Well, the excellent judge, which obviously I totally agree with that assessment of Judge Agius, dealt with -- or the Trial Chamber in Brdjanin dealt with at some length the question of newspaper articles in the context of a case, and this is of in the Trial Judgement in the 1st of September, 2004, headed general considerations regarding the evaluation of evidence. At paragraph 28, it dealt with hearsay evidence: "As regards hearsay evidence, the Trial Chamber reiterates that it's well settled in the practice and jurisprudence of this Tribunal that hearsay evidence is admissible. The approach taken by the Trial Chamber has been that since such evidence is admitted to prove the truth of its contents it ought to be satisfied that such evidence is reliable for that purpose in the sense of being voluntarily, truthful, and trustworthy and as appropriate." And then it goes on to say the probative value of a hearsay statement will depend upon the context and character of the evidence in question. The absence of the opportunity to cross-examine the person who made the statements, and whether the hearsay is first-hand or more removed has also been considered relevant to the probative value of the evidence. It's not the admission. It's the probative value. And then at paragraph 33, it dealt with -- specifically with newspaper articles. Your Honours will not be surprised to hear that they start by saying in that paragraph: "The Defence objects to all newspaper articles and reports introduced into evidence by the Prosecution submitting that they are unreliable and they amount to hearsay. Some of them come from hostile sources prone to propaganda and that the accused has not been given the opportunity of cross-examination or confrontation of evidence." Your Honours, they then -- exactly as what's been going on here. Your Honours, they then said, and, Your Honours, may I say straight away this is just a Trial Chamber decision, but it may help Your Honours when considering this. The Trial Chamber considers that when reliable newspaper reports and articles and similar items of evidence challenged may be important not only because they originate from the time of events they report upon but also because they very often corroborate the information provided by other evidence and confirm that the facts referred to are public and generally known. As such, they can be appropriate instruments for verifying the truth of the facts of a case." Your Honour, that's the background to the -- the evidence of the articles that were produced by Mr. Traynor. Now, Your Honours can I go back, please, to your decision on Mr. Traynor's, the admission of Mr. Traynor's evidence under 92, Rule 92 ter, if I can just find that for a moment, which I had. Your Honours gave a ruling on this matter on the 2nd of October of last year. And said in paragraph 12: "The Trial Chamber notes that the Prosecution identified what it considers to the relevant portions of the transcripts and statements for the witnesses. The Trial Chamber," and I quote, "has undertaken its own review of the evidence submitted and finds that for most witnesses the portions identified by the Prosecution are indeed relevant. The Trial Chamber does consider for some witnesses the Prosecution's indications are too inclusive and not related with the evidence of the witnesses. The Trial Chamber sets out below the portions." And you dealt with ST-155 and ST-198. With the exception of the portions identified above, the Trial Chamber is satisfied the transcripts and statements are relevant and probative and will therefore admit them. Paragraph 14: "The Prosecution tenders into evidence several documents that accompany the transcripts and statements of the witnesses. It submits that without those exhibits the witness's prior testimony cannot be fully evaluated for relevance and probative value, and then you deal with the fact that it must be on our exhibit list and that some -- some were included, others were not." And paragraph 15: "The Trial Chamber, in its review of the accompanying documents, finds that most of them do indeed form an inextricable and indispensable part of the evidence they accompany. Save for the following." And Your Honours then identified with ST-173 a number of documents. ST-180, and ST-183 Colonel -- ST-183, and then ST-189, the list of newspaper articles which was included. So excluded the list of newspaper articles. Your Honours, the test as enunciated partly there but also in, I think, Your Honours' first decision on the 2nd of October 2009, was the inextricable and indispensable part of the evidence they accompany. Your Honour, we had here the journalist - going back to the hearsay point for a moment - the journalist who actually wrote the articles and who testified that he had spoken to the people directly about what he recorded in those newspaper articles. He could have been cross-examined -- it's rare. Normally we don't have the journalist, for once we did. Mr. O'Sullivan, who had raised the original point, asked no questions at all in respect of how accurate his notes were or anything of that nature. Mr. Pantelic, on behalf of Zupljanin, raised the question of bias, Your Honour heard the answers, and in one or two occasions challenged the witness's notes of what he had said to Mr. Zupljanin. But they had here, effectively, someone who said, I spoke to these people and whom, in particular, Mr. Zupljanin, but also to the others whose statements I recorded direct into my articles. Now, Your Honours' ruling, and can I take entirely the point that was raised right at the beginning my address by Judge Delvoie, was on the basis - can I just find that for a moment, thank you. Yes, Your Honours ruled at page 10457 that: "We will admit into evidence the two statements made by the witness in 1999 and 2000 and that's it; that is to say, the 15 articles which were also part of the package will not be admitted into evidence. The reason is that we don't think they have sufficient evidentiary value. They're interesting articles, they're good, but we wouldn't rely on them for the purpose of reaching our conclusions in the case." Your Honours, that was despite, in fact, Mr. Pantelic, at page 10454, saying that he actually did not object to two of the articles, and I've forgotten which they are now. Your Honours, the reason for introducing this evidence was twofold. First, to rely on the truth of its contents given that they are newspaper articles and that they're hearsay. But, second, because of the notice that they provided to the leadership, in this case, in particular to Mr. Zupljanin, about what the international press was actually saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could I ask you to expand on that, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Because the -- one of the questions that immediately occurs to me at least, on that proposition, is that Mr. Traynor was a journalist for a newspaper from a particular country. In other words, there would have been a number of persons similarly placed, and the straight line that, as I understand it, you're seeking to draw between the newspaper articles and the -- the actions of the government seems to me to be a bit difficult to -- to make apart from the -- I suppose the basic argument that can be made about confusing sequence with consequence. But a government would have, by its nature have had --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: A press bureau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- been informed by a variety of sources, not least among them being its intelligence services and that of other agencies to which it would have had access. So what then becomes the magic, for want of a better word, of this particular journalist's story?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- magic is not that. But Your Honour knows that one of the issues in the case is what did either accused know about what was happening, in Mr. Zupljanin's case, within the area of the Autonomous Region, and, Mr. Stanisic, more generally. And, Your Honours, I anticipate, will hear evidence from the next witness that he, the next witness, specifically brought to the attention of Mr. Zupljanin -- now, I cannot say they were Mr. Traynor's articles particularly but articles that were being written in the international press about what was happening in Banja Luka. And this is just one example. And, Your Honours, one of the difficulties is if we want to put -- let us say that Mr. Zupljanin gave evidence, then if we wanted to put to him, Mr. Zupljanin, you were put on notice, weren't you, by this article, of Mr. Traynor, or other articles that we may have, that what was happening in Hambarine or in Kozarac was shelling. And people -- innocent people being carted off to camps. Now, if we don't have the article there, I can't show it to him, and that's the next problem I'm going to come onto with the way that the evidence came out, Your Honours, because -- and I direct Your Honours specifically to the parts where Mr. Traynor was asked about the articles, because we didn't realize that was going to be the ruling, the articles weren't read out at all. Mr. Traynor was asked about individual lines within those particular articles, and without the articles being in evidence it is impossible, when reading the transcript, to know what he is talking about. Your Honours, can I -- can I give you an example. Your Honours, he was shown, and I -- just find the transcript again. And, Your Honours, I should add that he was asked about his knowledge of languages and how he came to write his articles. But, Your Honours, for example, this is at page 10336 and on the screen was put his article, which is now 103583.03, and Ms. Pidwell said: "Sir, this isn't the first article you wrote in a series of three during your time in Visegrad, and my question is: "You refer -- you use the term 'Serbian irregulars' throughout. You can see it at the beginning and throughout the text. And I'm asking you if you'll explain what you mean by that?" Now, the problem is when we come back to this, which we may want to, particularly when we're dealing with Visegrad and whatever, we've no idea what the text is because Ms. Pidwell, for the reasons I've enunciated, that we thought that these articles were in, didn't go through it. So that's the first example. And it goes on like that, I'm afraid. He explain what he means by Serbian irregulars. Your Honour, the next one was at page 10354 of the transcript. Ms. Pidwell says: "Could I have 65 ter 3375, please. This is an article you wrote. It's dated the 29th of September. And in the second paragraph of the English you used the term 'ubiquitous police,' can you please expand on that?" Now, again, we don't know when we go back to this how the term "ubiquitous police" arises and in what context of the article. Your Honour -- and so -- and then she goes on the next page 10355: "And later in that article in paragraph four, you use a term 'a demented, crazed, and brutalised town,' can you expand on that, please?" Again, Your Honour, we can't see the context because we haven't got the article. And, Your Honour, when it comes, as I say, to the interview with Stojan Zupljanin, directly with the defendant, and Mr. Traynor has been cross-examined about that in -- it really is, we say, important that that article becomes an exhibit. So, Your Honours, I am sorry that I spent some time on general principles of hearsay, but in the context of this evidence we do ask you to reconsider your admission at least of the specific articles that Ms. Pidwell asked him about. She didn't ask him about all of them that were in the package so that when we come back to look at this transcript we can see what on earth it relates to. And that's really the upshot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: For the record, could you assist us by -- if not immediately, the -- you said the specific articles.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You're asking to us to reconsider which articles. As I said, if you aren't in a position to answer that immediately, if you could come back --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We understand the thrust of your --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if Your Honours are going to take a break, then I can give Your Honours the numbers immediately after the break of the actual articles she showed him, which are part of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or can I do it at some other -- if Your Honours want to ... to rise now, then I can do it at some other stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Can we anticipate a response from the Defence on this? The context in which we're asking this is whether we should take a break now and come back, or whether we should adjourn for -- for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Perhaps the solution is to sit five extra minutes. I can respond; then we can break. I will be very brief. And there's no point in breaking and coming back for -- for ten minutes, is what I'm suggesting. If the interpreters can survive for ten more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Are you ready to proceed, Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In a motion for reconsideration, the moving party must demonstrate that there's been an error of law or that there's been an injustice. Your Honours have ruled on the admission, or the inadmission -- inadmissibility of these articles in your -- in the transcript; pages 10457 to 10456 [sic]. And I include all those pages because after Judge Harhoff expressed the view of the Chamber, in turn, each of you expressed or gave explanations of the reasons why these articles are not admissible. There's been no suggestion and no showing that you abused your discretion because, under Rule 89(C), it is a matter of discretion for you whether or not hearsay is admissible. There has been no showing of that. You properly considered the submissions, you came to the conclusion on your own, and no one is suggesting that you made an error. So there's no basis for any second reconsideration. In fact, the Prosecution had a full-blown opportunity on the 18th of May, right after Traynor left, we had the contradictory and irreconcilable positions that it's for the truth of their contents/it's not for the truth of their contents. The confusion reigned at that point. So we say that it is furthermore incorrect, incorrect for the Prosecution to say that any one of the not-admitted articles could not be used in a future cross-examination. Well, of course, it could. If a witness took the stand, the Prosecution could show the witness one of the articles that Traynor wrote. Nothing precludes that by the fact that you didn't admit them through Traynor. So there's been no showing of abuse of your discretion, there's been no showing that you didn't apply the law correctly, and there's no basis for you to grant the second attempt at this reconsideration. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krgovic, did you wish to be heard on this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly only. In essence, what Ms. Korner says has nothing to do with the facts. The whole story about camps where prisoners were kept was -- started much earlier, before any -- by my -- by my client before any journalist arrived. So the possibility that this document may be shown to Zupljanin here -- in this trial has -- is not related to any facts. All the activities of Mr. Zupljanin relate to the period before the time described in Mr. Traynor's articles, so this is not a valid argument put forward by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Put forward by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I thought I heard an interruption. Just on the question of injustice, Mr. O'Sullivan says that we haven't shown injustice. I thought I'd made that clear. Because, Your Honours, Your Honours' ruling - and I forgot to read this part out, on this - was under paragraph 16: "The Trial Chamber will, when admitting into evidence the prior transcripts and written statements of a witness, will admit all the accompanying documents, save those identified herein above for the reason that it views this as an integral whole," and you accepted - or at least we thought you did - all the documents. And as a result, when Ms. Pidwell went through it, she didn't go into the detail she would have gone, had she known that they would not -- that the articles themselves would not go in. And as I pointed out, indeed, the whole transcript makes no sense now. So that's, we say, the reason why you should reconsider your ruling on at least those documents that the witness was specifically asked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we thank counsel for their assistance in this matter, and, of course, we should rule sometime next week. So we will take the adjournment now, to resume in Courtroom I at -- on Monday morning -- sorry, Tuesday morning - thank you - and, indeed, for -- straight through -- through the first week in June, we are all in morning sessions, unless there is some new change in the schedule. And I wish everyone a safe weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
